what_it_does: When training a massive language model across thousands of GPUs, the model is sliced into a chain of stages called a pipeline, and every GPU in that chain sits idle for a predictable stretch of time each round — a gap called a pipeline bubble. At 8,000 GPUs these bubbles can swallow more than 60% of all available compute. PipeFill uses those otherwise wasted gaps to run separate, unrelated jobs — batch inference requests or small training runs — achieving up to a 63% increase in useful work done per GPU, with less than 2% slowdown to the main training job.
method_in_detail:
The problem. Pipeline training works by splitting a model's layers across multiple machines. Each machine waits while the next one is busy, creating idle slots at both the start and end of every data batch. As you add more machines to train faster, the fraction of time wasted in these bubbles grows larger, not smaller. Adding a 8,000th GPU to cut training time from 50 to 26 days means each GPU is productive for less than 40% of its time.

The idea. PipeFill treats the bubbles as short-term GPU rentals. Instead of letting the hardware sit idle, it runs independent jobs — batch inference or small model training — inside those rental windows, then switches back to the main job the instant the bubble ends.

How it works. Three components collaborate. The Instrumented Pipeline Engine inserts a special 'bubble instruction' marker at known idle points in the pipeline schedule. At startup it measures exactly how long each bubble lasts and how much free memory the GPU has while the main job holds most of the memory. It then signals a parallel process — the Executor — each time a bubble begins. The Executor holds a pre-computed plan: it has profiled the fill job's computation graph and already decided which portions can finish within each bubble's time and memory budget. A greedy packing algorithm slices the fill job into pieces that fit. When the main job is running and memory is tight, the Executor can also quietly push the main job's optimizer state (rolling averages used by the Adam optimizer) to CPU memory and pull it back later, overlapping that transfer with parts of the main job that don't need it. The Scheduler sits above all this: it accepts incoming fill jobs, knows the bubble schedule across all GPUs, and assigns jobs to devices to match user-specified goals — shortest wait time, or highest overall throughput.

The result. On a simulated 40-billion-parameter language model training run scaled from 1,000 to 8,000 GPUs, PipeFill recovers 5–15% of idle GPU time at smaller scales and up to 63% at large scale, while slowing the main training job by less than 2%. At 8,000 GPUs the recaptured compute equals about 2,600 additional GPUs worth of work completed for free.
